concepts.title: Pressure in a Fluid and Hydrostatic Depth
concepts.definition: A fluid at rest pushes perpendicularly on any surface, with pressure defined as normal force per unit area. Pressure grows linearly with depth below a free surface: it equals the fluid density times gravity times the depth, and at one depth it pushes equally in all directions (Pascal's law).
concepts.key_idea: Deeper means more fluid overhead means more pressure -- the same everywhere at one depth.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph202.txt lines 40-200 (sections 9.1, 9.2 pressure, Pascal's law, variation of pressure with depth, atmospheric pressure, gauge pressure)

solution_steps.explain: The weight of the fluid column over unit area gives the gauge pressure.

concepts.title: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy
concepts.definition: A body submerged in a fluid feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. Whether an object floats or sinks is decided by comparing its average density with the fluid's: less dense bodies ride with part of their volume above the surface.
concepts.key_idea: Displaced fluid's weight is the buoyant force -- float if your density is lower than the fluid's.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph202.txt lines 130-260 (section 9.2 Archimedes' principle, buoyant force, floatation condition, hydrometers and balloons as applications)
question_patterns: state Archimedes' principle and define buoyant force

under what condition does a body float in equilibrium in a fluid

solution_steps.explain: The submerged part of the body determines how much fluid is pushed aside.
Density of fluid times displaced volume times gravity is the buoyant force, acting upward through the centre of buoyancy.
If buoyancy matches the full weight the body floats; a shortfall makes it sink, a surplus lifts it.

concepts.title: Streamline Flow and the Equation of Continuity
concepts.definition: In steady streamline flow each particle repeats the path of the one before it, without swirling. Because fluid cannot pile up anywhere, the volume crossing any cross-section per second is fixed: area times speed is constant, so a pipe's narrowing forces the fluid to speed up.
concepts.key_idea: What enters per second must leave per second -- narrow the pipe and the current must quicken.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph202.txt lines 261-360 (section 9.3 streamline flow, equation of continuity, flow rate idea, critical velocity and turbulence mention)
question_patterns: find the speed of flow where the pipe narrows

distinguish streamline flow from turbulent flow

solution_steps.explain: Entry area times entry speed is the volume delivered per second.
Splitting the same flow rate over the smaller exit area raises the speed.

concepts.title: Bernoulli's Principle and Torricelli's Efflux
concepts.definition: Where a fluid moves faster its pressure drops -- Bernoulli's principle trades pressure for speed plus height along a streamline. Its famous corollary, Torricelli's law, gives the speed of liquid escaping a hole at depth h as the square root of 2 g h, exactly as if the parcel had fallen freely through h.
concepts.key_idea: Faster flow costs pressure -- and a hole at depth h fires liquid at free-fall speed.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph202.txt lines 361-470 (section 9.4 Bernoulli's principle and theorem, applications, speed of efflux, Torricelli's law, venturi and atomiser mention)
question_patterns: state Bernoulli's principle and name one application

solution_steps.explain: Free fall through the depth supplies the squared efflux speed.
The root is the escaping liquid's speed.

concepts.title: Viscosity, Stokes' Law and Terminal Speed
concepts.definition: Viscosity is internal friction between fluid layers, strongest in thick liquids like honey. A sphere creeping through a viscous fluid feels a drag given by Stokes' law, six pi times viscosity times radius times speed; falling balls therefore reach a steady terminal speed where drag plus buoyancy equals weight.
concepts.key_idea: Drag rises with speed until it cancels gravity -- then the fall continues at constant terminal speed.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph202.txt lines 471-570 (section 9.5 viscosity, coefficient of viscosity, Stokes' law, terminal velocity derivation, Reynolds number)
question_patterns: state Stokes' law and the condition for its use
in class 11 mechanical properties of fluids: find the terminal speed of the given sphere in the given liquid
why does a raindrop fall with nearly constant speed
how does terminal speed depend on the radius of the ball
define coefficient of viscosity and its units
what role does buoyancy play in the terminal speed balance

solution_steps.explain: Weight pulls down; buoyancy and viscous drag push up against the fall.
At terminal speed the net force vanishes: drag equals weight minus buoyancy.
Solving the balance gives a terminal speed proportional to the square of the radius and to the density difference, and inversely to the viscosity.

concepts.title: Surface Tension and Surface Energy
concepts.definition: A liquid surface behaves like a stretched skin: molecules at the surface lack neighbours on one side, so the surface minimises its area. Surface tension measures the force per unit length across any line in the surface, and stretching a surface stores energy equal to tension times the extra area created -- the basis of capillary rise and droplet shapes.
concepts.key_idea: Surface tension is force per length and energy per area at once -- the surface works to shrink itself.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph202.txt lines 571-700 (section 9.6 surface tension, surface energy, angle of contact, capillary rise, excess pressure in drops and bubbles)
question_patterns: define surface tension and give its units

solution_steps.explain: The work done to create extra surface is surface tension times the added area.
